From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Buck (crater)

Buck

| Location | [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus") |
| Coordinates | [5°45′S 349°36′E﻿ / ﻿5.75°S 349.6°E﻿ / -5.75; 349.6](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Buck_(crater)&params=5.75_S_349.6_E_globe:venus_type:landmark) |

![}](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Buck_crater_PIA00470.jpg/330px-Buck_crater_PIA00470.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**Buck** is a crater in the [Navka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navka_Planitia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Navka Planitia (page does not exist)") region of [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"). It has the [terraced walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraced_wall "Terraced wall"), flat radar-dark floor, and central peak that are characteristic of craters classified as "complex". The central peak on its floor is unusually large. Flow-like deposits extend beyond the limits of the coarser rim deposits on its west and southwest. Like about half of the craters mapped by *[Magellan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_(spacecraft) "Magellan (spacecraft)")* to date, it is surrounded by a local, radar-dark halo.

**Edith Newbold Wharton** ([/ˈhwɔːrtən/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); née **Jones**; January 24, 1862 – August 11, 1937) was an American writer and designer. Wharton drew upon her insider's knowledge of upper-class New York society to portray, realistically, the lives and morals of the [Gilded Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilded_Age "Gilded Age"). In 1921, she became the first woman to win the [Pulitzer Prize for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Fiction "Pulitzer Prize for Fiction") for her novel *[The Age of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Age_of_Innocence "The Age of Innocence")*. She was inducted into the [National Women's Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Hall_of_Fame "National Women's Hall of Fame") in 1996.[[1]](#cite_note-1) Her other well-known works are *[The House of Mirth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_House_of_Mirth "The House of Mirth")*, the novella *[Ethan Frome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethan_Frome "Ethan Frome")*, and several notable ghost stories.

## Biography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edith_Wharton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edith_Wharton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Edward_Harrison_May_-_Edith_Wharton_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/250px-Edward_Harrison_May_-_Edith_Wharton_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Harrison_May_-_Edith_Wharton_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg)

Portrait of Wharton as a child by [Edward Harrison May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Harrison_May "Edward Harrison May") (1870)

Edith Newbold Jones was born on January 24, 1862, to George Frederic Jones and Lucretia Stevens Rhinelander, at their [brownstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brownstone "Brownstone") at 14 West 23rd Street in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), New York City.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200816-2)[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDwight199412–13-3) To her friends and family, she was known as "Pussy Jones".[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinkel2012-4) She had two elder brothers, Frederic Rhinelander and Henry Edward.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200816-2) Frederic married [Mary Cadwalader Rawle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Cadwalader_Rawle_Jones "Mary Cadwalader Rawle Jones"); their daughter was landscape architect [Beatrix Farrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrix_Farrand "Beatrix Farrand"). Edith was [baptized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptized "Baptized") April 20, 1862, [Easter Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Sunday "Easter Sunday"), at [Grace Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Church_(Manhattan) "Grace Church (Manhattan)").[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200816-2)

Wharton's paternal family, the Joneses, were a very wealthy and socially prominent family, having made their money in real estate.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200821-5) The saying "[keeping up with the Joneses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeping_up_with_the_Joneses "Keeping up with the Joneses")" is said to refer to her father's family.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200822-6)[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenstock1994216-7) She was related to the [Rensselaers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manor_of_Rensselaerswyck "Manor of Rensselaerswyck"), the most prestigious of the old [patroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patroon "Patroon") families, who had received land grants from the former Dutch government of New York and New Jersey. Her father's first cousin was [Caroline Schermerhorn Astor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Schermerhorn_Astor "Caroline Schermerhorn Astor").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200834-8) Fort Stevens, in New York, was named for Wharton's maternal great-grandfather, [Ebenezer Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebenezer_Stevens "Ebenezer Stevens"), a [Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War") hero and general.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200818-9)

Wharton was born during the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"). However, in describing her family life, Wharton does not mention the war, except that their travels to Europe after the war were due to the depreciation of American currency.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee200816-2)[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee20087–8-10) From 1866 to 1872, the Jones family visited France, Italy, Germany, and Spain.[[11]](#cite_note-Chronology-11) During her travels, the young Edith became fluent in [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_(language) "French (language)"), [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_(language) "German (language)"), and [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_(language) "Italian (language)"). **Ida Bell Wells-Barnett** (July 16, 1862 – March 25, 1931) was an American [investigative journalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investigative_journalism "Investigative journalism"), [sociologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology"), educator, and early leader in the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement_(1896–1954) "Civil rights movement (1896–1954)"). She was one of the founders of the [National Association for the Advancement of Colored People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_for_the_Advancement_of_Colored_People "National Association for the Advancement of Colored People") (NAACP).[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiddings,_''Encyclopedia''2013-1) Wells dedicated her career to combating prejudice and violence, and advocating for African-American equality—especially for women.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''NYTs'',_Dickerson,_Mar._9,20184F-2)

Throughout the 1890s, Wells documented [lynching of African-Americans in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynching_in_the_United_States "Lynching in the United States") in articles and through pamphlets such as *Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in all its Phases* and *The Red Record*, which debunked the fallacy frequently voiced by whites at the time – that all Black lynching victims were guilty of crimes. Wells exposed the brutality of lynching, and analyzed its sociology, arguing that whites used lynching to terrorize African Americans in the [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States") because they represented economic and political competition—and thus a threat of loss of power—for whites. She aimed to demonstrate the truth about this violence and advocate for measures to stop it.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiddings,_''When_and_Where_I_Enter,''1984-3)

Wells was born into [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States") in [Holly Springs, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly_Springs,_Mississippi "Holly Springs, Mississippi"). She was freed as an infant under the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation"), when [Union Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Army "Union Army") troops captured Holly Springs. At the age of 16,[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoses,1978109-4) she lost both her parents and her infant brother in the [1878 yellow fever epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Mississippi_Valley_yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1878 "Lower Mississippi Valley yellow fever epidemic of 1878"). She got a job teaching and kept the rest of the family together with the help of her grandmother, later moving with some of her siblings to [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"). Soon, Wells co-owned and wrote for the *[Memphis Free Speech and Headlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Free_Speech_and_Headlight "Memphis Free Speech and Headlight")* newspaper, where her reporting covered incidents of [racial segregation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States "Racial segregation in the United States") and inequality. Eventually, her investigative journalism was carried nationally in [Black-owned newspapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_newspapers "African-American newspapers"). Subjected to continued threats and criminal violence, including when a white mob destroyed her newspaper office and presses, Wells left Memphis for [Chicago, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois"). She married [Ferdinand L. Barnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Lee_Barnett_(Chicago) "Ferdinand Lee Barnett (Chicago)") in 1895 and had a family while continuing her work writing, speaking, and organizing for civil rights and the [women's movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights_in_the_United_States "Women's rights in the United States") for the rest of her life.

Wells was outspoken regarding her beliefs as a Black female activist and faced regular public disapproval, sometimes including from other leaders within the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement_(1865–1896) "Civil rights movement (1865–1896)") and the [women's suffrage movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage_in_the_United_States "Women's suffrage in the United States"). She was active in [women's rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_rights "Women's rights") and the women's suffrage movement, establishing several notable women's organizations. A skilled and persuasive speaker, Wells traveled nationally and internationally on lecture tours.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWells_Papers,_Univ._Chicago-5) Wells died on March 25, 1931, in Chicago, and in 2020 was posthumously honored with a [Pulitzer Prize special citation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards") "for her outstanding and courageous reporting on the horrific and vicious violence against African Americans during the era of lynching."[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPulitzer2020-6)

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ida_B._Wells&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Ida_B._Wells-Barnette_Brith_Home_%28Holly_Springs%2C_MS%29.jpg/250px-Ida_B._Wells-Barnette_Brith_Home_%28Holly_Springs%2C_MS%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ida_B._Wells-Barnette_Brith_Home_(Holly_Springs,_MS).jpg)

The [Bolling–Gatewood House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolling–Gatewood_House "Bolling–Gatewood House"). The Wells family lived in [slave quarters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_quarters_in_the_United_States "Slave quarters in the United States") located behind the house of [Spires Boling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spires_Boling "Spires Boling") while enslaved to him, now a museum focused on Wells

Ida Bell Wells was born on the Boling Farm near [Holly Springs, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly_Springs,_Mississippi "Holly Springs, Mississippi").[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcKinney-7) Born on July 16, 1862, Ida Wells was the first child of James Madison Wells (1840–1878) and Elizabeth "Lizzie" (Warrenton). James Wells was born to an enslaved woman named Peggy and Peggy's white enslaver, thus he was enslaved under the doctrine of *[partus sequitur ventrem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partus_sequitur_ventrem "Partus sequitur ventrem")*. When James was 18, his father brought him to Holly Springs, hiring him out as a carpenter's apprentice to architect [Spires Boling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spires_Boling "Spires Boling"), with James's wages going to his enslaver. One of ten children born on a [plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantation_complexes_in_the_Southern_United_States "Plantation complexes in the Southern United States") in Virginia, Lizzie was [abducted and trafficked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slave_trade_in_the_United_States "Slave trade in the United States") away from her family and siblings and tried without success to locate her family following the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcMurry-8) Lizzie was owned by Boling for domestic labor in his home, now the [Bolling–Gatewood House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolling–Gatewood_House "Bolling–Gatewood House"). Before the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation") was issued, both of Wells's parents were enslaved to Boling, and thus Ida was also born enslaved. James Wells built much of the Bolling–Gatewood house, in which Boling lived, and which in March 2002[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIBW_Museum,_) became the Ida B. Wells–Barnett Museum.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMatthews,_Dasha-10) The Wells family lived elsewhere on the property. Ground plans on display in the Ida B. Wells–Barnett Museum identify shacks behind the house as the residence of the Wells family.

After [emancipation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_slavery_in_the_United_States "End of slavery in the United States"), James became a trustee of the newly established Shaw University (now [Rust College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_College "Rust College")) in Holly Springs. He refused to vote for [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Democrats "Southern Democrats") candidates during the period of [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era"), became a member of the [Loyal League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyal_League "Loyal League"), and was known as a "race man" for his involvement in politics and his commitment to the [Republican Party](ht

**Ellen Anderson Gholson Glasgow** (April 22, 1873 – November 21, 1945) was an American novelist who won the [Pulitzer Prize for the Novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_the_Novel "Pulitzer Prize for the Novel") in 1942 for her novel [*In This Our Life*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_This_Our_Life_(novel) "In This Our Life (novel)").[[1]](#cite_note-1) She published 20 novels, as well as short stories, to critical acclaim. A lifelong Virginian, Glasgow portrayed the changing world of the [contemporary South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States#History "Southern United States") in a [realistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism "Literary realism") manner, differing from the idealistic escapism that characterized Southern literature after [Reconstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_era "Reconstruction era").[[2]](#cite_note-docsouth.unc.edu-2)

## Early and family life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ellen_Glasgow&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early and family life")]

Born in [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia"), on April 22, 1873, to Anne Jane Gholson (1831-1893) and her husband, Francis Thomas Glasgow, the young Glasgow developed differently from other women of her aristocratic class.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Due to poor health (later diagnosed as chronic heart disease), Glasgow was educated at home in Richmond, receiving the equivalent of a high school degree, although she read deeply in philosophy, social and political theory, as well as European and British literature.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Her parents married on July 14, 1853, survived the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), and would have ten children together, of whom Ellen would be the next to youngest. Her mother, Anne Gholson, was inclined to what was then called "nervous invalidism"; which some attributed to her having borne and cared for ten children.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Glasgow also dealt with "nervous invalidism" throughout her life.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Ellen Glasgow thought her father self-righteous and unfeeling.[[7]](#cite_note-7) However, some of her more admirable characters reflect a [Scots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people")-[Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinist "Calvinist") background like his and a similar "iron vein of [Presbyterianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterian "Presbyterian")".[[8]](#cite_note-8)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Ellen_Glasgow_House_%28Richmond%2C_Virginia%29.jpg/250px-Ellen_Glasgow_House_%28Richmond%2C_Virginia%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ellen_Glasgow_House_(Richmond,_Virginia).jpg)

The [Ellen Glasgow House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Glasgow_House "Ellen Glasgow House") in Richmond, Virginia, where Ellen Glasgow lived since the age of 13 and did much of her writing. It is a National Historic Landmark.

Ellen Glasgow spent many summers at her family's [Louisa County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_County,_Virginia "Louisa County, Virginia"), estate, the historic [Jerdone Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerdone_Castle "Jerdone Castle") [plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plantations_in_the_American_South "Plantations in the American South"), which her father bought in 1879, and would later use that setting in her writings.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Her paternal great-grandfather, Arthur Glasgow, had emigrated with his brothers in 1776 from Scotland to the then-large and frontier [Augusta County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusta_County,_Virginia "Augusta County, Virginia"). Her father, Francis Thomas Glasgow, was raised in what had become [Rockbridge County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockbridge_County,_Virginia "Rockbridge County, Virginia"), graduated from Washington College (now [Washington and Lee University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_and_Lee_University "Washington and Lee University")) in 1847, and would eventually manage the [Tredegar Iron Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tredegar_Iron_Works "Tredegar Iron Works").[[10]](#cite_note-10) Those had been bought in 1848 by Glasgow's maternal uncle, [Joseph Reid Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_R._Anderson "Joseph R. Anderson"), who had graduated fourth in his class of 49 from [West Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point "West Point") in 1836 and would introduce the labor of skilled and enslaved Africans at the ironworks to accompany skilled white workers. Anderson was a major business and political figure in Richmond, who supported the [Confederate States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America"), joined the [Army of Northern Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_Northern_Virginia "Army of Northern Virginia"), and attained the rank of general.[[11]](#cite_note-11) However, because the Tredegar Ironworks produced munitions crucial to the Confederate cause, General [Robert E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Lee "Robert E. Lee") asked General Anderson to return and manage the ironworks rather than lead armies in the field.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

Her mother was Anne Jane Gholson (1831-1893), born to William Yates Gholson and Martha Anne Jane Taylor at [Needham plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Needham_(Farmville,_Virginia) "Needham (Farmville, Virginia)") in [Cumberland County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumberland_County,_Virginia "Cumberland County, Virginia"). Her grandparents were Congressman [Thomas Gholson, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gholson,_Jr. "Thomas Gholson, Jr.") and Anne Yates, who descended from [Rev. William Yates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Yates_(college_president) "William Yates (college president)"), the [College of William & Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_William_&_Mary "College of William & Mary")'s fifth president (1761–1764).[[13]](#cite_note-Roberts-13) Gholson was descended from [William Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Randolph "William Randolph"), a prominent colonist and land owner in the [Commonwealth of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Virginia "Commonwealth of Virginia"). He and his wife, Mary Isham, were sometimes referred to as the "Adam and Eve" of Virginia.[[13]](#cite_note-Roberts-13)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ellen_Glasgow&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Portrait_of_E._Glasgow.jpg/250px-Portrait_of_E._Glasgow.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_E._Glasgow.jpg)

Portrait of Ellen Glasgow

During more than four decades of literary work, Glasgow published 19 novels, a collection of poems, a book of short stories, and a book of literary criticism. Her first novel, *The Descendant* (1897) was written in secret and published anonymously when she was 24 years old. She destroyed part of the manuscript after her mother died in 1893. Publication was further delayed because her brother-in-law and intellectual mentor, George McCormack, died the following year. Thus Glasgow completed her novel in 1895.[[14]](#cite_note-14) It features an emancipated heroine who seeks passion rather than marriage. Although it was published anonymously, her authorship became well known the following year, when her second novel, *Phases of an Inferior Planet* (1898), announced on its title page, "by Ellen Glasgow, author of *The Descendant*".

By the time *The Descendant* was in print, Glasgow had finished *Phases of an Inferior Planet*.[[15]](#cite_note-15) The novel portrays the demise of a marriage and focuses on "the spirituality of female friendship".[[16]](#cite_note-16) Critics found the story to be "sodden with hopelessness all the way though",[[17]](#cite_note-17) but "excellently told".[[18]](#cite_note-18) Glasgow stated that her third novel, *The Voice of People* (1900) was an objective view of the poor-white farmer in politics.[[19]](#cite_note-19) The hero is a young Southerner who, having a genius for politics, rises above the masses and falls in love with a higher class girl. Her next novel, *The Battle-Ground* (1902), sold over 21,000 copies in the first two weeks after publication.[[20]](#cite_note-20) It depicts the South before and during the Civil War and was hailed as "the first and best realistic treatment of the war from the southern point of view."[[21]](#cite_note-21)

[![Title Page of The Deliverance (1904)](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/The_Deliverance_title_page_%281904%29.png/250px-The_Deliverance_title_page_%281904%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Deliverance_title_page_(1904).png)

*The Deliverance* (1904)

Much of her work was influenced by the romantic interests and human relationships that Glasgow developed throughout her life. *[The Deliverance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Deliverance "The Deliverance")* (1904) and her previous novel, *The Battle-Ground*, were written during her affair with "Gerald B.", her long-time secret lover. They "are the only early books in which Glasgow's heroine and hero are united" by the novels' ends.[[22]](#cite_note-22) *The Deliverance*, published in 1904, was the first Glasgow book to garner popular success.[[23]](#cite_note-23) The novel portrays a romance built on the dramatic relationship between the hero and the heroine due to traditional class constraints. The hero is an aristocrat turned into a common laborer after the events of the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), and the heroine lacks the aristocratic lineage but obtains aristocratic qualities such as education and refinement.[[24]](#cite_note-Godbold_64-24) The genuine affection and reconciliation of the romance of the two were attempts by Glasgow to prove that "traditional class consciousness should be inconsequential to love affairs."[[24]](#cite_note-Godbold_64-24) *The Deliverance* criticizes the institution of marriage because Glasgow herself faced social barriers that prevented her from marrying at that time. *The Deliverance* is notable for offering "a naturalistic treatment of class conflicts" that emerge after Reconstruction, providing realistic views of social changes in Southern literature.[[2]](#cite_note-docsouth.unc.edu-2)

Glasgow's next four novels were written in what she considered her "earlier manner"[[25]](#cite_note-25) and received mixed reviews. *The Wheel of Life* (1906) sold moderately well based on the success of *The Descendant*. Despite its commercial success, however, reviewers found the book disappointing.[[26]](#cite_note-26) Set in New York (the only novel not set in Virginia), the story tells of domestic unhappiness and tangled love affairs.[[27]](#cite_note-27) It was unfavorably compared to [Edith Wharton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edith_Wharton "Edith Wharton")'s *[House of Mirth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Mirth "House of Mirth")*, which was published that same year. Most critics recommended that Glasgow "stick to the South".[[28]](#cite_note-28) Glasgow regarded the novel as a failure.[[29]](#cite_note-29)

*The Ancient Law* (1908) portrayed white factory workers in the Virginia textile industry,[[30]](#cite_note-30) and analyzes the rise of industrial capitalism and its corresponding social ills.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Critics considered the book overly melodramatic.[[32]](#cite_note-32) With *The Romance of a Plain Man* (1909) and *The Miller of Old Church* (1911) Glasgow began concentrating on gender traditions; she contrasted the conventions of the Southern woman with the feminist viewpoint,[[33]](#cite_note-33) a direction which she continued in *Virginia* (1913).

As the United States women's [suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage "Suffrage") movement was developing in the early 1900s, Glasgow marched in the English suffrage parades in the spring of 1909. Later she spoke at the first suffrage meeting in Virginia and was an early member of the [Equal Suffrage League of Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Suffrage_League_of_Virginia "Equal Suffrage League of Virginia").[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35) Glasgow felt that the movement came "at the wrong moment" for her, and her participation and interest waned.[[36]](#cite_note-36) Glasgow did not at first make women's roles her major theme, and she was slow to place heroines rather than heroes at the centers of her stories.[[37]](#cite_note-37) Some called her *Virginia* (1913; about a southern lady whose husband abandons her when he achieves success), *Life and Gabriella* (1916; about a woman abandoned by a weak-willed husband, but who becomes a self-sufficient, single mother who remarries well), and *Barren Ground* (1925); discussed below, her "women's trilogy". Her later works have heroines who display many of the attributes of women involved in the political movement.

**Edna Ferber** (August 15, 1885 – April 16, 1968) was an American novelist, short story writer and playwright. Her novels include the [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize")-winning *[So Big](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Big_(novel) "So Big (novel)")* (1924), *[Show Boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_Boat_(novel) "Show Boat (novel)")* (1926; made into the celebrated [1927 musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_Boat "Show Boat")), *[Cimarron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimarron_(novel) "Cimarron (novel)")* (1930; adapted into the [1931 film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimarron_(1931_film) "Cimarron (1931 film)") which won the [Academy Award for Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture")), *Giant* (1952; made into the [1956 film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_(1956_film) "Giant (1956 film)") of the same name) and *Ice Palace* (1958), which also received a [film adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_Palace_(film) "Ice Palace (film)") in 1960. She helped adapt her short story "[Old Man Minick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Man_Minick "Old Man Minick")", published in 1922, into a play (*[Minick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minick "Minick")*) and it was thrice adapted to film, in 1925 as the silent film *[Welcome Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_Home_(1925_film) "Welcome Home (1925 film)")*, in 1932 as *[The Expert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Expert_(1932_film) "The Expert (1932 film)")*, and in 1939 as *[No Place to Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Place_to_Go_(1939_film) "No Place to Go (1939 film)")*.

## Life and career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edna_Ferber&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Early years

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edna_Ferber&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Ferber was born August 15, 1885, in [Kalamazoo, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalamazoo,_Michigan "Kalamazoo, Michigan"), to a Hungarian-born Jewish storekeeper, Jacob Charles Ferber, and his [Milwaukee, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee,_Wisconsin "Milwaukee, Wisconsin")–born wife, Julia (Neumann) Ferber, who was of German Jewish descent. The Ferbers had moved to Kalamazoo from [Chicago, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago,_Illinois "Chicago, Illinois"), in order to open a dry goods store, and her older sister Fannie had been born there three years earlier.[[1]](#cite_note-ferber-auto-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert20001-3) Ferber's father was not adept at business,[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerber193918-4) and the family moved often during Ferber's childhood. From Kalamazoo, they returned to Chicago for a year, and then moved to [Ottumwa, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottumwa,_Iowa "Ottumwa, Iowa"), where they resided from 1890 to 1897 (ages 5 to 12 for Ferber).

In Ottumwa, Ferber and her family faced brutal [anti-Semitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Semitism "Anti-Semitism"), including adult males verbally abusing, mocking and spitting on her on days when she brought lunch to her father, often mocking her in a [Yiddish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish "Yiddish") accent.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerber193941-5)[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7) According to Ferber, her years in Ottumwa "must be held accountable for anything in me that is hostile toward the world".[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerber193931-8) During this time, Ferber's father began to lose his eyesight, necessitating costly and ultimately unsuccessful treatments.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerber193951-9) At the age of 12, Ferber and her family moved to [Appleton, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin "Appleton, Wisconsin"), where she graduated from high school and later briefly attended [Lawrence University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_University "Lawrence University").

### Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edna_Ferber&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

After graduation, Ferber planned to study elocution, with vague thoughts of someday becoming an actress, but her family could not afford to send her to college. On the spur of the moment, she took a job as a [cub reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cub_reporter "Cub reporter") at the *[Appleton Daily Crescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Post-Crescent "The Post-Crescent")* and subsequently moved to the *[Milwaukee Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Journal "Milwaukee Journal").*[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2000428-10)[[7]](#cite_note-:0-7) In early 1909, Ferber suffered a bout of anemia and returned to Appleton to recuperate. She never resumed her career as a reporter, although she subsequently covered the [1920 Republican National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Republican_National_Convention "1920 Republican National Convention") and [1920 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Democratic_National_Convention "1920 Democratic National Convention") for the [United Press Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Press_Association "United Press Association"), and newspaper work was a theme in her first novel, *Dawn O'Hara, The Girl Who Laughed*, and the later *Cimarron.*[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGilbert2000423-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

While Ferber was recovering, she began writing and selling short stories to various magazines, and in 1911 she published her first novel, *Dawn O'Hara, The Girl Who Laughed*. In 1912, a collection of her short stories was published in a volume titled *Buttered Side Down*. In her autobiography, Ferber wrote:[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFerber1939171-172-13)

> In that day, and for a girl in her early twenties, they were rather hard tough stories... The book got good reviews. I was startled and grimly pleased when some of the reviewers said that obviously these stories had been written by a man who had taken a feminine nom de plume as a hoax. I have always thought that a writing style should be impossible of sex determination; I don't think the reader should be able to say whether a book has been written by a man or a woman.

In 1925, she won the [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize "Pulitzer Prize") for her book *[So Big](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Big_(novel) "So Big (novel)")*. Ferber initially believed her draft of what would become *So Big* lacked a plot, glorified failure, and had a subtle theme that could easily be overlooked. When she sent the book to her usual publisher, [Doubleday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubleday_(publisher) "Doubleday (publisher)"), she was surprised to learn that he greatly enjoyed the novel. This was reflected by the several hundreds of thousands of copies of the novel sold to the public.[[14]](#cite_note-:2-14) Following the award, the novel was made into a [silent film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent_film "Silent film") starring [Colleen Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleen_Moore "Colleen Moore") that [same year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Big_(1924_film) "So Big (1924 film)"). A remake followed in [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Big_(1932_film) "So Big (1932 film)"), starring [Barbara Stanwyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Stanwyck "Barbara Stanwyck") and [George Brent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Brent "George Brent"), with [Bette Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bette_Davis "Bette Davis") in a supporting role. A [1953 version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Big_(1953_film) "So Big (1953 film)") of *So Big* starring [Jane Wyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Wyman "Jane Wyman") is the most popular version to modern audiences.[[14]](#cite_note-:2-14)

Riding the popularity of *So Big*, Ferber's next novel, *[Show Boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_Boat_(novel) "Show Boat (novel)")* in 1926, was just as successful. Shortly after its release, composer [Jerome Kern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Kern "Jerome Kern") proposed turning it into a [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_Boat "Show Boat"). Ferber was shocked, thinking it would be transformed into a typical light entertainment of the 1920s. It was not until Kern explained that he and [Oscar Hammerstein II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Hammerstein_II "Oscar Hammerstein II") wanted to create a different type of [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theater "Musical theater") that Ferber granted him the rights and it premiered on [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theater "Broadway theater") in 1927, and it has been [revived](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revival_(theatre) "Revival (theatre)") eight times.

Her 1952 novel *Giant* became the basis of the [1956 movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant_(1956_film) "Giant (1956 film)"), starring [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), [James Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Dean "James Dean") and [Rock Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Hudson "Rock Hudson").[[14]](#cite_note-:2-14)

Plaque located in Manhattan, at 65th Street & Central Park West, in the building in which Edna Ferber lived for six years

Ferber was reportedly the first author to assign film rights to her books on short-term contracts so that the rights needed to be renegotiated regularly.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

### Death

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edna_Ferber&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Death")]

Ferber died at her home in New York City, of [stomach cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomach_cancer "Stomach cancer"),[[16]](#cite_note-16) at the age of 82. She left her estate to her sister and nieces.[[17]](#cite_note-brody-17)

## Personal life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Edna_Ferber&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Ferber never married, had no children, and is not known to have engaged in a romance or sexual relationship.[[a]](#cite_note-18) In her early novel *Dawn O'Hara*, the title character's aunt remarks, "Being an old maid was a great deal like death by drowning – a really delightful sensation when you ceased struggling." Ferber did take a maternal interest in the career of her niece [Janet Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janet_Fox "Janet Fox"), an actress who performed in the original Broadway casts of Ferber's plays *[Dinner at Eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinner_at_Eight_(play) "Dinner at Eight (play)")* (1932) and *[Stage Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_Door_(play) "Stage Door (play)")* (1936).

Ferber was known for being outspoken and having a quick wit. On one occasion, she led other Jewish guests in leaving a house party after learning the host was antisemitic.[[17]](#cite_note-brody-17) Once, after [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noël_Coward "Noël Coward") joked about how her suit made her resemble a man, she replied, "So does yours."[[6]](#cite_note-:1-6)

**Margaret Munnerlyn Mitchell** (November 8, 1900 – August 16, 1949)[[2]](#cite_note-2) was an American novelist and journalist. Mitchell wrote only one novel that was published during her lifetime, the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War")-era novel *[Gone with the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone_with_the_Wind_(novel) "Gone with the Wind (novel)")*, for which she won the [National Book Award for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Fiction#Most_Distinguished_Novel_(1935–1936) "National Book Award for Fiction") for Most Distinguished Novel of 1936[[3]](#cite_note-nyt1937-3) and the [Pulitzer Prize for Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Fiction "Pulitzer Prize for Fiction") in 1937. Long after her death, a collection of Mitchell's girlhood writings and a novella she wrote as a teenager, titled *[Lost Laysen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Laysen "Lost Laysen")*, were published. A collection of newspaper articles written by Mitchell for [*The Atlanta Journal*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlanta_Journal-Constitution "The Atlanta Journal-Constitution") was republished in book form.

## Family history

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Margaret_Mitchell&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Family history")]

Margaret Mitchell was a lifelong resident of [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"). She was born in 1900 into a wealthy and politically prominent family. Her father, [Eugene Muse Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Muse_Mitchell "Eugene Muse Mitchell"), was an attorney, and her mother, [Mary Isabel "Maybelle" Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maybelle_Stephens_Mitchell "Maybelle Stephens Mitchell"), was a [suffragist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffragist "Suffragist") and [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") activist. She had two brothers, Russell Stephens Mitchell, who died in infancy in 1894, and Alexander Stephens Mitchell, born in 1896.[[4]](#cite_note-cyclopedia-4)[[5]](#cite_note-seven_sisters-5)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/74/Eugene-Muse-Mitchell.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eugene-Muse-Mitchell.jpg)

Eugene Muse Mitchell, the father of Margaret Mitchell

Mitchell's family on her father's side were descendants of Thomas Mitchell, originally of [Aberdeenshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeenshire "Aberdeenshire"), Scotland, who settled in [Wilkes County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilkes_County,_Georgia "Wilkes County, Georgia") in 1777, and served in the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"). Thomas Mitchell was a surveyor by profession. He was on a surveying trip in [Henry County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_County,_Georgia "Henry County, Georgia"), at the home of John Lowe, about 6 miles from [McDonough, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonough,_Georgia "McDonough, Georgia"), when he died in 1835 and is buried in that location.[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) Thomas Mitchell's son, William Mitchell, born December 8, 1777, in [Edgefield County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgefield_County "Edgefi

All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#) _(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#))_ As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Venus&action=edit§ion=23#)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5) Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ( [141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ( [131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and Distribution of named craters in the Solar System as of 2017.[1][2][3][4][a]

This is a list of craters on Venus, named by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature. All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[1][2] *(For features on Venus other than craters see, list of montes on Venus and List of coronae on Venus.[3])*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[1] fewer than the lunar and Martian craters but more than on Mercury.[4][5][6][a]

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include Callisto (141), Ganymede (131), Rhea (128), Vesta (90), Ceres (90), Dione (73), Iapetus (58), Enceladus (53), Tethys (50) and Europa (41). For a full list, *see List of craters in the Solar System*.
